Bond price

Show me the workings

STEP BY STEP
  1. Build the payments.
    Coupon per period = Face value × Annual coupon rate ÷ m

  2. Discount each payment to today.
    Price = Σ Cash flowt / (1 + y/m)t

    Σ means add all payments. y is annual yield as a decimal, m is payments per year, and t is the payment number.

  3. Add the present values.
    Price = C × [1 − (1 + r)−N] / r + F × (1 + r)−N

    C = coupon per period; F = face value; r = y/m; N = number of periods. At zero yield, Price = C × N + F.

The terms, in plain English

Coupon rate
The annual payment as a percentage of face value. A 5% coupon on 1,000 pays 50 a year, even if the market price changes.
Yield to maturity (YTM)
The discount rate that makes the value of all promised payments equal to the price. It includes coupons and the gain or loss between purchase price and redemption. Realised returns can differ, for example if coupons are reinvested at a different rate or the issuer defaults.
Current yield
Annual coupon cash ÷ current price. It measures coupon income relative to price, but ignores the gain or loss at maturity.
Present value (PV)
What a future payment is worth today after discounting at the required yield.
Macaulay duration
The average time until you receive the bond’s payments, weighted by each payment’s present value. It is not usually the same as maturity.
Modified duration
A measure of price sensitivity. A modified duration of 4 means a 1 percentage-point yield rise produces roughly a 4% price fall. This approximation is best for small changes.

A small model, with clear boundaries.

Fixed coupons, fixed redemption at face value, and valuation on a coupon date immediately after payment. No accrued interest, defaults, calls, fees or taxes. A single yield discounts every cash flow. This is a learning model, not a live bond quote.

Duration, convexity & solver conventions

Macaulay duration = Σ(time in years × present value) / price. Modified duration = Macaulay duration / (1 + y/m). Convexity = Σ[t(t+1) × PV] / [price × m² × (1+y/m)²]. Here t counts periods and y is a decimal annual yield. For a small change Δy, ΔP/P ≈ −modified duration × Δy. Larger changes need convexity or full repricing. Yield is solved by bisection; it is not a guarantee of realised return.
